items.title: Anthropic publishes 'Discovering cryptographic weaknesses with Claude' on Wednesday July 29 — the Claude Mythos Preview model, working over roughly 60 hours with a human researcher, derived an end-to-end key-recovery attack on HAWK-256 (dropping the smallest-key attack cost from 2^64 to 2^38 operations and effectively halving HAWK's security level) and a 200–800x speedup for the best known attack on seven-round AES-128; the HAWK team subsequently withdrew HAWK from NIST's additional post-quantum signature standardization process
items.summary: Anthropic's research post 'Discovering cryptographic weaknesses with Claude,' published Wednesday July 29, 2026 with coverage across CSO Online, The Hacker News, CyberScoop, Decrypt, and Matthew Green's Cryptographic Engineering blog, describes two original cryptographic-analysis results produced with the pre-release Claude Mythos Preview model on Amazon Bedrock's gated research preview. The first is a full end-to-end key-recovery attack on HAWK-256, a lattice-based post-quantum digital signature candidate that had been under NIST's additional-signature standardization process for the two years since 2024. The attack found a previously unknown nontrivial automorphism in HAWK's underlying Lattice Isomorphism Problem, dropping the cost of recovering the smallest key from about 2^64 operations to 2^38 — effectively halving HAWK's security level and requiring substantially larger key sizes to restore the intended security margin (which erases most of HAWK's efficiency advantage relative to competing candidates). The specific timing detail is that Mythos improved the best known attack in roughly 60 hours of collaborative work with a human researcher, after HAWK had survived two years of expert human review. The second result is a 200- to 800-fold speedup of the best-known attack on a research seven-round variant of AES-128 (real-world AES-128 uses 10 rounds; the seven-round version is a standard target for cryptanalysis research). Anthropic coordinated disclosure with NIST and the HAWK team before publishing; the HAWK team confirmed the finding and withdrew HAWK from NIST's additional post-quantum signature standardization process on the basis of the attack. Neither result compromises any deployed production system — real-world 10-round AES remains unaffected, and HAWK had not yet been standardized or deployed — but the results are the first published instances of a frontier LLM producing original novel-attack cryptanalysis results at a level that had escaped years of expert human review.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: two reads. First, the specific 'frontier LLMs are now producing publishable original math/cryptography research, not just re-derivations' read: the specific concrete data point is that Mythos found a nontrivial automorphism in HAWK's Lattice Isomorphism Problem that expert human cryptographers had missed over two years of NIST review — and it did so in roughly 60 hours of collaborative work with a human. That is the specific first widely-documented case of an LLM producing an attack that (a) genuinely improves the state of the art, (b) is coordinated-disclosed with NIST like a real cryptography finding, and (c) forces a real-world action (HAWK withdrawn from standardization). For a Python developer, the practical implication is that the specific mental model of 'LLMs are useful for coding help but not for original research' has to update — Mythos here is doing something structurally different, and Anthropic's decision to publish the methodology alongside the results is worth reading as an example of what LLM-driven research disclosure looks like. Second, the specific 'the boring boring parts of the finding are the most important' read: the AES-128 result affects a seven-round research variant, not the 10-round production standard, and the HAWK result affects a candidate that had not been deployed. That specific pattern is what responsible disclosure of AI-discovered cryptanalysis is supposed to look like — the safeguards worked, the disclosure worked, and no production system is at risk. For a hobbyist coder, the specific action item is to internalize that current deployed cryptography (AES-256, AES-128 at 10 rounds, RSA, elliptic curve, and the already-standardized post-quantum ML-KEM/ML-DSA) remain unaffected by these findings — but the specific class of vulnerability discovery is now something LLMs can meaningfully participate in, which is a durable change to the discipline's threat model.

items.title: Visual Studio Code 1.131 ships Wednesday July 29 with the new Agent Host Protocol architecture (a dedicated host process that runs Copilot, Claude, and Codex agent harnesses side by side behind a common protocol), running-subagent visibility (model name, elapsed time, active tool call in the main conversation), built-in dictation across chat/editors/terminal without the Speech extension, and a new hybrid Markdown editor for the Agents window
items.summary: Microsoft released Visual Studio Code 1.131 on Wednesday July 29, 2026, per code.visualstudio.com/updates/v1_131 and coverage across InfoWorld ('VS Code 1.131 zeroes in on subagents') and Visual Studio Magazine. The release's headline change is architectural: VS Code is rearchitecting how agent sessions work around a dedicated 'agent host' process, based on the new Agent Host Protocol (AHP), which lets multiple agent harnesses — GitHub Copilot, Anthropic's Claude, OpenAI's Codex — run side by side inside VS Code behind a common protocol interface rather than each shipping its own custom integration. Enabling it requires opting into chat.agentHost.enabled. The subagent-visibility change surfaces the model name, elapsed time, and the tool call each running subagent is actively executing directly in the main conversation view, so a developer can see what a spawned subagent is doing without opening its conversation. The built-in dictation change moves speech transcription from the separate Speech extension into the core workbench, making dictation available in chat inputs, all text editors, and the integrated terminal without a supplementary install. The hybrid Markdown editor change adds an alternate view for the new Agents window that lets you view, edit, and add agent-actionable comments to Markdown files with rendered preview and raw source side by side. The 1.131 release also refines chat.agent tool-permission prompts and improves how session mode is restored when resuming a paused agent.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: two reads. First, the specific 'Agent Host Protocol turns the editor into a real multi-agent host, not a Copilot-only surface' read: the specific new architecture is that AHP is a documented protocol boundary between the editor and any agent harness, which means Claude, Codex, Copilot, and future agents talk to VS Code through the same interface. For a Python developer, the practical implication is that switching between agent providers stops being an install-a-new-extension-and-relearn-the-UI experience — the same run/pause/resume/tool-permission UI works for any AHP-conformant harness, and the same subagent-visibility view applies whether the subagent is a Copilot spawn, a Claude Code subagent, or a Codex worker. That specific interoperability layer is the same design pattern MCP applies to tools (see the AM's MCP 2026-07-28 sibling item) — a well-scoped protocol between one client and many providers — and this is the second live example this week of that pattern being applied to a different problem inside the same broader agentic-development stack. Second, the specific 'built-in dictation is a small change with a real accessibility and workflow implication' read: moving dictation out of an extension and into the workbench means the specific latency of dictating into a terminal or chat input drops from 'install and configure a third-party extension' to 'available in the fresh install.' For a hobbyist coder, the practical action item is to try dictating into the terminal or into a chat prompt with one hand while looking at the code with the other — the specific new workflow that a built-in dictation surface enables is the specific reason to update to 1.131 today.

items.title: GitHub Copilot CLI v1.0.76 ships Thursday July 30 — new enable/disable controls for plugins, custom instructions, agents, LSP servers, and hooks (so a developer can turn any subset of the harness off for a session without editing config), plus first-class support for xAI's Grok 4.5 model, tighter sandbox enforcement of denied paths on macOS and Linux, unsent prompt text preserved within sessions, and restored session-mode on resume
items.summary: GitHub released Copilot CLI v1.0.76 on Thursday July 30, 2026, per github.com/github/copilot-cli/releases and the Havoptic release-tracker. The headline user-facing change is a set of new session-level enable/disable controls: a developer can now turn off plugins, custom instructions, subagents, LSP servers, or hooks for a specific Copilot CLI session without editing any config files. That specific granularity matters because the previous behavior — either fully-enabled or fully-disabled per install — made debugging a misbehaving plugin or hook awkward and made 'run without any of my customizations' require a separate profile. The model-support change is the addition of first-class support for xAI's Grok 4.5 alongside the existing model roster (GPT-5.6 family, Claude Opus 5 / Sonnet 5, Gemini 3.6 Flash); Grok 4.5 is the model xAI released on July 8, 2026 at Opus-class capability at lower cost. The security-related changes tighten sandbox enforcement on macOS and Linux so that denied-path violations are enforced at the syscall boundary (previously a workflow could sometimes traverse into a denied path indirectly through a symlink), preserve unsent prompt text within a Copilot session so an accidental terminal blur does not lose in-progress input, restore session mode (agent vs chat vs review) when resuming a paused session, and improve the URL permission prompt so that the domain being requested is clearly labeled before the developer approves fetch access. The Copilot CLI v1.0.76 release ships behind the same GitHub Copilot Business and Enterprise licensing that governs the existing Copilot CLI installation base.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: two reads. First, the specific 'per-session enable/disable is the ergonomics fix Copilot CLI needed to be trustworthy for real work' read: any developer who has run a coding-agent session and found a plugin or hook interfering — the pre-commit hook that runs the wrong linter, the custom instruction that changed the output style, the subagent that spawned before you wanted it to — knows the specific frustration of not being able to turn just that one thing off without a config-file round-trip. The new controls make the specific 'run this session with everything else disabled' workflow one flag away, which is the specific ergonomic pattern that separates a real agentic-development tool from a novelty. For a Python developer, the practical implication is that the specific integration friction of pairing Copilot CLI with an unfamiliar codebase drops materially — you can start clean, add plugins one at a time, and reproduce a bug against a known configuration. Second, the specific 'Grok 4.5 as a first-class Copilot model is the meaningful data point' read: the specific reason Grok 4.5 landing in Copilot CLI matters is that it makes the specific 'multi-provider agent stack' pattern real — VS Code 1.131 (sibling item) added AHP so Copilot, Claude, and Codex run side by side inside the editor, and Copilot CLI 1.0.76 adds Grok 4.5 as a peer to the existing Copilot models. The specific implication is that developers who want to comparison-test the frontier providers on the same Copilot workflow now have four families (OpenAI GPT-5.6, Anthropic Claude 5, Google Gemini 3.6 Flash, xAI Grok 4.5) directly addressable from one CLI. For a hobbyist coder, the specific action item is to try running the same coding task through two different model providers in Copilot CLI and observe how the specific style of output — the tool-calling patterns, the code-suggestion patterns, the failure modes — differs; that comparison is now materially cheaper to run than it was yesterday.

items.title: Simon Willison publishes 'Adding a custom MCP server to Claude and ChatGPT' as a TIL on Tuesday July 28 (updated Wednesday July 29) — a step-by-step walkthrough of adding an unauthenticated MCP server to both Claude's + menu 'Add custom connector' modal and ChatGPT's Developer-mode custom-connector flow, using Willison's own read-only SQL-over-blog-database MCP server as the worked example, and flagging the specific ChatGPT-side complication that the flow requires enabling Developer mode in the Security and login panel before the MCP option is visible
items.summary: Simon Willison published 'Adding a custom MCP server to Claude and ChatGPT' on his TIL site on Tuesday July 28, 2026, with a Wednesday July 29 update. The post is a hands-on walkthrough of the specific end-to-end steps for adding an unauthenticated MCP server as a custom connector to both Claude and ChatGPT's web chat surfaces, timed to the MCP 2026-07-28 spec release (see the AM's sibling item) and the corresponding Anthropic 'Bringing MCP 2026-07-28 to Claude' announcement. On the Claude side, Willison notes the flow is relatively straightforward: click the + menu next to the chat prompt, choose 'Add custom connector,' and paste in the MCP server URL with optional auth details. On the ChatGPT side, he documents the specific extra step that a developer has to first enable 'Developer mode' in the Security and login panel of ChatGPT settings before the 'Add custom connector' option appears at all — a friction point that has been undocumented until this post. The worked example Willison uses is an unauthenticated MCP server that exposes read-only SQL queries against a copy of his own site's database (a common personal-project shape). The post is the third in a running series of Willison MCP-integration walkthroughs and joins the specific class of 'the first person who successfully wired up X writes down the specific steps' documentation that MCP has needed since the client ecosystem started fragmenting.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: two reads. First, the specific 'this is the practical companion to the MCP 2026-07-28 spec news you already read this morning' read: the AM item covered the spec release, Anthropic's overnight commitment to bring MCP 2026-07-28 to Claude Desktop / Claude on the web / the Claude API, and the specific SEP 2468 OAuth issuer-validation fix. What Willison's TIL adds is the specific concrete workflow a developer needs to actually add their own MCP server to the two most-used chat surfaces — Claude web and ChatGPT web — including the specific undocumented ChatGPT Developer-mode gate. For a Python developer who has been thinking about writing an MCP server for a personal project (a database wrapper, a home-network status API, a scratchpad tool) but has not yet done the last-mile integration into the chat client, this post is the specific missing-manual that takes an hour off the first attempt. Second, the specific 'the pattern Willison uses — an unauthenticated read-only SQL-over-blog-database server — is a great template' read: exposing a read-only view of your own SQLite / Postgres database as an MCP server is a specific safe on-ramp to the MCP world that lets you get useful natural-language queries over your own data without any of the auth complexity that a public MCP server would carry. For a hobbyist coder who runs a small personal site or logs personal data into a SQLite file, the specific action item is to spend an hour on this pattern this weekend — the read-only-SQL-over-my-own-DB shape is a legitimately useful personal tool and a good specific project to learn the current MCP client-integration ergonomics against.

items.title: The Federal Communications Commission approves rules on Tuesday July 28 banning imports of new Chinese-manufactured humanoid and quadruped robots and connected power inverters — the trigger cited is documented backdoors in Unitree quadrupeds already deployed at MIT and Princeton and the wormable BLE-based UniPwn root-access exploit affecting Unitree Go2 / B2 / G1 / H1 platforms; already-approved units may continue to receive updates through January 1, 2029 with FCC authority to revisit; China holds approximately 85% of the global humanoid-robot market
items.summary: The FCC approved and released rules on Tuesday July 28, 2026 banning imports of new humanoid and quadruped robots manufactured in China, along with connected power inverters used in renewable-energy systems and data-center equipment. Coverage across CBS News, Forbes, The Hill, TechSpot, PBS NewsHour, and The AI Insider converges on the specific mechanism: the FCC has revoked authorization for new units of these product classes from a covered list of Chinese manufacturers (Unitree, Ubtech, Xiaomi's CyberDog, and others). Two specific security incidents are cited as the immediate trigger: (a) documented backdoors in Unitree robots already deployed on university campuses, including MIT and Princeton, that allowed remote data exfiltration and remote control; and (b) the UniPwn Bluetooth Low Energy exploit disclosed earlier in July that grants root-level access to Unitree Go2 and B2 quadrupeds and G1 and H1 humanoids and that is wormable (a compromised unit can infect other units within BLE range). Products already authorized for sale in the US are not immediately affected — they can continue to operate and receive updates through January 1, 2029, though the FCC retains authority to revisit those authorizations if new security concerns surface. The FCC's rules are expected to accommodate waivers for products from non-Chinese suppliers and for Chinese-designed products whose manufacturers commit to on-shore US assembly. The direct-effect data point is that China holds approximately 85% of the global humanoid-robot market, with Unitree alone accounting for close to 20% of the specific humanoid segment. The rules take effect immediately for new imports and are one of the strongest China-specific hardware-decoupling actions of the current administration.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: two reads. First, the specific 'this is not a policy story, it is a security story that has been forcing itself into policy' read: the specific triggers cited by the FCC — documented backdoors on university-deployed Unitree units and the wormable UniPwn BLE exploit — are exactly the kind of security-incident data points that would justify the same action if the manufacturer were domestic. For a Python developer following the specific 'consumer AI hardware runs a full computer with a full network stack and needs to be treated like one' theme, the specific practical implication is that a specific class of consumer robot has been formally reclassified as untrusted-network-endpoint from a US-federal perspective — the same way certain routers and video-surveillance cameras were reclassified in the 2020s. The specific technical detail worth internalizing is that UniPwn is a Bluetooth Low Energy vulnerability that grants root access without any authentication, which is the same class of vulnerability that has affected consumer IoT devices for years — the pattern here is that consumer-robot firmware has not yet matured to the specific baseline that the FCC now expects. Second, the specific 'the 85% market-share number tells you that this is going to reshape the US robotics ecosystem in a real way' read: with roughly 85% of the global humanoid supply chain running through China, an import ban on new units means the specific US robotics startups — Figure, Agility, Apptronik, Boston Dynamics — pick up the demand that would otherwise have gone to Unitree, Ubtech, or Xiaomi. For a hobbyist coder, the specific action item is to note that the specific pre-order backlogs at Figure and Agility are about to grow — and that the specific software stacks those US-manufactured humanoids run (which are much more Python-heavy than the Chinese-manufactured equivalents) will get correspondingly more attention from the third-party developer ecosystem.

items.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT for Academic Researchers on Wednesday July 29 — a program giving up to 100,000 selected academic researchers free access by 2027 to the full GPT-5.6 family (Sol, Terra, Luna) plus expanded deep-research quotas, larger context windows, and higher usage limits inside ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex; the initial cohort starts with 10,000 researchers this summer at institutions including the Institute for Advanced Study and École normale supérieure; each participant can invite four collaborators; the program is backed by a $250 million commitment through 2027
items.summary: OpenAI announced ChatGPT for Academic Researchers on Wednesday July 29, 2026, per openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-academic-researchers and coverage across Axios ('OpenAI launches free AI access program for academic researchers'), SiliconANGLE, Dataconomy, and Business Standard. The specific mechanism: verified academic researchers at eligible institutions apply for free access to frontier OpenAI models — the GPT-5.6 family (Sol, Terra, Luna) at launch — with expanded deep-research quotas, higher usage limits, and larger context windows than the ordinary free or paid ChatGPT tiers, delivered inside ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex. The initial rollout in summer 2026 covers 10,000 researchers, with the Institute for Advanced Study (Princeton) and École normale supérieure (Paris) already onboarded. OpenAI's stated intent is to scale to 100,000 researchers by 2027. Each participating researcher can invite four collaborators from the same institution, so the effective seat count is up to 500,000. Eligibility requires verification of institutional affiliation and submission of active research-project details plus intended scientific use of the platform. Model weights remain off-limits — the program provides API and product access, not open-weights distribution. OpenAI positioned the program as part of a broader $250 million commitment through 2027 to external scientific research and discovery, and framed it explicitly alongside the July 20 Jacobian-Conjecture-counterexample result (in which Levent Alpöge used Claude Fable 5 to construct the specific counterexample to a 1939 open problem) as evidence of what frontier-model access unlocks for working academic researchers.
items.why_it_matters: For Gabe: two reads. First, the specific 'this is OpenAI's first-mover response to Anthropic's academic partnerships and Google DeepMind's AlphaEvolve rollout' read: the specific new data point is that OpenAI is committing $250 million through 2027 and structuring a specific 100,000-seat academic program, which is materially larger than any prior academic-access rollout from a frontier lab. For a Python developer with hobbyist interest in AI research applications, the specific practical implication is that the specific class of research code being written this year — Jupyter notebooks driving GPT-5.6 API calls in the deep-research configuration, Codex-produced code for scientific simulations, the specific pattern of 'grad student uses frontier model as a research collaborator' — is now sponsored infrastructure rather than a per-lab budget expense, which means the volume of published-in-the-open academic experiments with frontier models is about to increase materially. Second, the specific 'the specific institutions OpenAI led with are worth reading as intent-signaling' read: leading with the Institute for Advanced Study (Princeton) and École normale supérieure (Paris) — two of the most mathematically-serious pure-research institutions in the world — signals that OpenAI wants the early results of this program to look like the specific Jacobian-Conjecture-counterexample class of finding (pure math, formal verification, disproving an 87-year-old open problem) rather than the specific 'help me draft a grant proposal' class of use. For a hobbyist coder, the specific action item is that the specific research artifacts coming out of this program will be public-facing (papers, Lean proofs in the DeepMind Formal Conjectures repo, arXiv preprints) and worth watching as a real-world signal of what frontier-model-plus-expert-researcher pairs can produce at scale.
items.why_it_matters_brief: OpenAI's ChatGPT for Academic Researchers gives 10,000 → 100,000 researchers free GPT-5.6 family access with expanded deep research and higher limits, backed by $250M through 2027 — a step-change in academic-model access above prior per-lab arrangements.

source.name: OpenAI — Accelerating scientific discovery with ChatGPT for Academic Researchers

revisions.change: created — OpenAI announced ChatGPT for Academic Researchers Wednesday July 29; program provides free access to the GPT-5.6 family (Sol, Terra, Luna) plus expanded deep-research quotas, higher usage limits, and larger context windows across ChatGPT / ChatGPT Work / Codex to verified academic researchers; initial rollout summer 2026 covers 10,000 researchers including Institute for Advanced Study (Princeton) and École normale supérieure (Paris); target of 100,000 researchers by 2027; each participant can invite four collaborators (up to 500,000 effective seats); requires institutional-affiliation verification and active-research-project details; model weights remain off-limits — API/product access only; $250M commitment through 2027; framed alongside July 20 Jacobian Conjecture counterexample as evidence of the specific research use case; coverage across OpenAI, Axios, SiliconANGLE, Dataconomy, Business Standard, TechTimes, ETIH EdTech News, StudioGlobal AI
